headline: Plant your garlic this week — late October is the zone 6a window to get cloves in before the ground freezes.

tasks.title: Plant garlic
tasks.detail: Break a head into cloves and plant pointy-end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart, in a sunny, well-drained bed. This is your last good window before the soil locks up; they root now and sprout next spring.

tasks.title: Pick the frost-sweetened crops
tasks.detail: Kale, Brussels sprouts, carrots, parsnips and leeks all get sweeter after a frost or two, so keep harvesting them. Pull any remaining tender crops (the last green tomatoes, peppers, squash) before a hard freeze hits.

tasks.title: Mulch garlic and perennials
tasks.detail: After planting garlic, cover the bed with 3-4 inches of straw or shredded leaves. Mulch around perennials and strawberries too once the ground gets cold — it insulates roots against the freeze-thaw cycles of a coastal winter.

tasks.title: Shut off and drain outdoor water
tasks.detail: Disconnect, drain and store hoses, and shut off any outdoor spigots or rain barrels before the first hard freeze. Water left in them expands when it freezes and cracks the pipe or barrel.

tasks.title: Put beds to bed
tasks.detail: Clear out spent annual plants and fallen fruit, especially anything that looked diseased this year (blighted tomato vines, powdery-mildew squash). Compost the healthy stuff and trash the diseased to avoid overwintering spores.

tasks.title: Stockpile leaves and top up compost
tasks.detail: Rake fallen leaves and either shred them for mulch or layer them into the compost pile with kitchen scraps. A few inches of compost or chopped leaves spread over empty beds now feeds the soil over winter.
